newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian prime minister sees more personnel changes. [CORRECTED 22:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Russian prime minister sees more personnel changes. [CORRECTED 22:00 GMT]

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said further changes in the administration were to come after last month's sweeping cabinet reshuffle which brought in or promoted a number of leading reformers.

"The renovated government is already practically formed," he told Moskovsky Komsomolets (corrects from Ekho Moskvy) newspaper and RIA news agency in an interview published on Sunday. "Today four vacancies remain unfilled. It's possible there may be other personnel changes too."
The head of the State Tax Service was reported on Saturday to have tendered his resignation to Chernomyrdin, although there was no word on whether it would be accepted.
The premier repeated his determination to end non-payment of pensions and public sector wages and restore growth to the Russian economy after five years of decline.

He said the government could already show results. The federal payments backlog had more than halved since the start of the year, he said, and the remaining 2.7 trillion roubles ($475 million) would be paid off in six weeks to two months.
Tax collection was also a priority, Chernomyrdin said.
"Preliminary results for the first quarter of this year give grounds for hope," he went on, saying that while there was no noticeable economic growth, there had been no dramatic decline.
"I am sure that we have realistic possibilities to make a breakthrough in the economic situation this year," he said.

The prime minister defended the Union Treaty signed with Belarus last week, saying the government had no intention of damaging the Russian economy by merging it with its poorer neighbour, where free market reforms have scarcely taken root.

"We are talking about synchronising economic reforms," he said. "And that doesn't mean Russia withdrawing from hard-won positions or marking time but, on the contrary, pulling our neighbours' transformation processes up to the Russian level."
"No one is going to hang Belarus's problems round the neck of the Russian budget," Chernomyrdin said.
The treaty signed by presidents Boris Yeltsin and Alexander Lukashenko on Wednesday was vague. The detail of the union will be in a charter to be published for public debate this month.

Chernomyrdin rejected media suggestions that the governments had tried to sew up a deal in private. He said talk of a split in the Russian government between liberal opponents of the Belarus treaty and conservative backers was mistaken, though there were differences of opinion in cabinet.
Kremlin sources have said Chernomyrdin supported a more ambitious union treaty but that this was blocked by last-minute opposition led by his liberal first deputy, Anatoly Chubais.

Among the liberals' complaints were that Lukashenko has taken a hard line with opponents and clamped down on the media. Chernomyrdin said he would not judge how democratic Belarus was but would respect the will of the people who elected Lukashenko.
Chernomyrdin repeated his rejections of foreign and Russian media reports last week that he had amassed great wealth.
The premier insisted his only income was his four million rouble ($700) monthly salary and that he owned no shares in Gazprom, the gas giant he headed before taking office in 1992.
He suggested these and previous allegations of corruption in the Russian administration were part of an orchestrated scheme by unnamed rivals to discredit the government and Russia itself.

"In essence, this article is, of course, an element in a huge, well orchestrated and planned game against both Russian business and, in the final analysis, against Russia and Russian interests," the prime minister said.
